Title: The Future of Scheduling in Athena on HPCs

Abstract. The large increase in luminosity expected from Run 4 of the LHC
presents the ATLAS experiment with a new scale of computing challenge, and
we can no longer restrict our computing to CPUs in a High Throughput Com-
puting paradigm. We must make full use of the High Performance Computing
resources available to us, exploiting accelerators and making eﬃcient use of
large jobs over many nodes. Here we describe current developments in intro-
ducing these capabilities to Athena, ATLAS’s general software framework.
1 ATLAS Computing Requirements and HPCs
The ATLAS [1] experiment is one of the two general purpose experiments at the LHC, ex-
ploring the frontiers of High Energy Physics with a combination of precision measurements
of Standard Model parameters and searches for Beyond the Standard Model physics. The
experiment is currently preparing for an upgrade during the next long shutdown period to
prepare for the High Luminosity upgrade of the LHC, where an approximately 3x increase in
instantaneous luminosity is expected.
To date, ATLAS has focused on the LHC computing grid and other High Throughput
Computing resources to fulﬁl its computing needs. These closely match the requirements
of the experiment, providing a large number of CPU cores which can each independently
process individual collision event, since there are no dependencies between these events.
However, the large increase in collected data expected from the High Luminosity upgrade
means the experiment can no longer rely on just these resources, but must also make full use
of the High Performance Computing (HPC) resources available.
These HPCs have a few diﬀerences which distinguish them from conventional Grid re-
sources. Most notably as regards the scheduling choices made by ATLAS:
• Grid resources are CPU centric, with accelerators rarely even being provided. On the other
hand HPCs often rely on accelerators (namely GPUs) for the majority of their computa-
tional power, and we must make use of these accelerators to make full use of the resource.
• Grid resources provide jobs of less than one node, and primarily 8 or 16 core execution
slots. HPCs, on the other hand, generally provide whole node queues, with a preference

2 Athena
The ATLAS experiment makes use of a uniﬁed framework for all of its computing needs, and
this framework is called Athena [2]. Athena is a specialization of the experiment-independent
Gaudi [3] framework, and divides the processing that must be done on each (collision) event
into a set of tasks called algorithms, with dependencies between these algorithms expressed
by declaring the data that each algorithm takes as input and writes as output. These depen-
dencies are then used to deﬁne a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of algorithms that is repeated
for each event. In this work, we will use the term task to refer to the execution of a speciﬁc
algorithm on a speciﬁc event.
Athena uses Intel’s TBB [4] to deﬁne a pool of threads (one per available CPU core)
and schedule tasks that are ready (i.e. whose input data dependencies are all satisﬁed) onto
threads as they become free. Figure 1 illustrates this paradigm. Each job generally processes
a large number of events in parallel to ensure the threads are always kept busy.

In this paradigm the algorithms themselves are given the task of scheduling work onto
GPUs. Since the Athena scheduler is unaware of this the CPU core remains blocked while
the GPU work runs, and stays idle if the algorithm does not make use of that CPU time itself.
3 Multi-Node Scheduling
Our ﬁrst task, therefore, is to deal with multi-node jobs. In particular, we want to be able to
run a job that processes a very large number of events on a job spanning multiple nodes.
The simplest way to do this would be to pre-split the events among the various nodes (i.e.
static scheduling). However, this leads to nodes becoming starved of work near the end of
a job, since the events assigned to some nodes will, by chance, ﬁnish faster than the events
assigned to another node. When this happens the nodes that ﬁnish their work faster remain
allocated to the job (and continue to accrue charges) until all nodes complete their work.
Meanwhile, integrating the nodes entirely and unifying the scheduling of tasks onto
threads on all nodes also poses performance problems. In particular, if a task which takes
input data that was processed on one node were scheduled onto another node, the input data

3.1 Architecture and Technology Choice
At CHEP 2023 [7] we demonstrated related work, where we made use of HPX [8] both to
schedule events to speciﬁc nodes, and to schedule individual tasks on those nodes. The design
of HPX encourages the use of a model where work is pushed to nodes without any regard to
how busy those nodes already are. In that work we showed that when we tried to scale beyond
even a few nodes we experienced serious performance issues due to a couple of reasons:
• The push model means work is pushed to nodes which may already be fairly busy, while
another node may be left idle longer than necessary. This is not ideal for load balancing.
• The on-node handling of new event assignments was done on the same thread pool that
handles compute work. As a result a task to assign a new event could get stuck in the
queue for a signiﬁcant amount of time, causing severe latency issues.
While debugging these issues, we also learned that modern HPCs (and in particular,
NERSC’s Perlmutter, the HPC we are developing on) often require the use of MPI [9] to
make full use of the high-speed internal network.
We therefore decided to make some architectural modiﬁcations, and to use MPI as the
communication protocol between nodes. On each node, we then use TBB to manage the
local thread pool.

In the new architecture, the processes on each node (launched using an appropriate MPI-
aware mechanism) individually start up and initialize, determining the work to be done by the
entire job, and reading any necessary conﬁgurations and auxiliary data. After running this
initialization and initializing MPI, the processes are then synchronized across the job.
Each worker process then sends one message to the manager process per worker thread,
requesting assignment of an event. As event assignments are received, the dedicated sched-
uler thread on the worker process reads the assigned events and adds them to the local pool.
Thereafter, whenever an event is completed, the worker process will request a replacement
event from the manager process.
The manager process, meanwhile, acts as a server and assigns events to workers only upon
request. This pull architecture ensures that events are well balanced among the workers, since
a faster worker (or one that by chance receives events that are quicker to process) will request
replacement events more often than a slower worker.
In addition, all reading and writing of event data is done by the workers individually.
This greatly reduces the total network traﬃc, but requires a merging step at the end of the job
to merge the output of the workers into a single set of ﬁles. Further planned work includes
determining whether the optimal strategy is this one, or one where the workers return the
completed work to the manager process which would then handle writing.
3.2 Implementation and Performance
Multi-node scheduling has been implemented in Athena as a new mode of operation that we
call AthenaMPI, analogous to two existing modes of operation, AthenaMP [10] (which uses
multiple forked processes on a single machine) and AthenaMT [5] (which uses multithread-
ing on a single machine). It has been implemented using B.MPI3 [11] and has been tested
on NERSC’s Perlmutter using Cray MPICH [12], and on an individual machine with both
MPICH [13] and OpenMPI [14]. The implementation can be found in our fork of Athena
here.
Figure 3 illustrates how using our multi-node scheduler throughput scales almost per-
fectly at least up to the thousands of cores level.
4 Asynchronous Scheduling
Our second task is to implement functionality to enable work to be scheduled onto accelera-
tors such as GPUs without blocking a CPU core.
In order to avoid requiring special implementations for each accelerator architecture, we
chose to forgo the concept of accelerator (or GPU) algorithms in favour of introducing a
general concept of an asynchronous algorithm. This is an alternative type of algorithm that
can internally make calls to asynchronous oﬄoading APIs (such as the CUDA streams API)
and await the results of these calls without blocking the thread they run on.
The bulk of this implementation was put into Gaudi, and a more detailed description can
be found in the proceedings for our ACAT 2024 talk [15].

lightweight thread API much like TBB tasks. Unlike (classic1) TBB tasks, ﬁbers act as

4.2 Athena Speciﬁcs
Athena makes use of a mechanism called StoreGate to retrieve, manage, and write out event
data. This mechanism uses a thread local variable to track which event a given thread is
currently processing. When all algorithms are synchronous, this poses no problem since
the variable can be set when the task begins executing and can be relied upon to remain un-
changed until the task has ﬁnished. With asynchronous algorithms, however, the ﬁber may be
suspended and the thread used for another ﬁber working on a diﬀerent event. In addition when
the ﬁber is resumed it may be on a diﬀerent thread to that on which it was originally running.
We therefore additionally cache this information in a ﬁber local variable before beginning to
execute an asynchronous algorithm, and provide a restoreAfterSuspend function which
restores the thread local variable used by the StoreGate mechanism.
Since we are now relying on the algorithms to include a call to restoreAfterSuspend
after each suspension (the point at which the ﬁber would resume), as a courtesy to users we
envision including this call in wrappers that interface various oﬄoading APIs with the Boost
Fiber based asynchronous algorithm framework. We have implemented one such wrapper for
CUDA streams.
5 Future Work
We have started integrating the work presented here into the production Athena framework.
This will allow us to begin testing the new functionality at scale.
With AthenaMPI, we plan to determine whether it would be useful to centralize the writ-
ing of output, eliminating the merge step that is currently required.
With asynchronous algorithms, we will extend the wrapper functionality to other GPU
APIs (e.g. AMD’s HIP) and the remote machine learning inference functionality that is
currently being developed as AthenaTriton [17].
